lines.text: From one of humanity's oldest ancestors to kings who carved churches from rock and an empire that never bowed. This is the story of Ethiopia.
More than three million years ago, a small female walked upright here. Found in 1974 and named Lucy, she changed what we know of our ancestors.
Around the first century, the Kingdom of Aksum rose in the highlands, minting its own coins and trading with Rome and India.
Its people raised great carved stone obelisks, towering markers of Aksum's wealth and power.
In the fourth century Aksum turned to Christianity, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church became one of the oldest churches in the world.
In Aksum stands the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, where Ethiopian Christians believe the Ark of the Covenant is kept.
In the east, the walled city of Harar grew into a centre of Islamic learning, with dozens of mosques.
Around 1200, eleven churches were cut downward out of solid rock at Lalibela. Pilgrims still gather there today.
By 1270 a new line of rulers held the highlands, at the heart of the land we know as Ethiopia.
Their Christian empire would last seven centuries, one of the very few African states never colonised for long.
Its emperors claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and called themselves the Solomonic dynasty.
From Ethiopia's highlands came the coffee plant. By the fifteenth century it was brewed in Yemen, and the world soon followed.
In the seventeenth century the emperors settled at Gondar and built castles there for their court.
In 1844 Menelik the Second was born. He would expand the realm, found a new capital and defend it against Europe.
In 1886 he founded Addis Ababa, the new flower, still the capital today.
Haile Selassie, born in 1892, would become the last emperor, and lead Ethiopia into the modern age.
In 1896 Menelik's army crushed an Italian force at Adwa. Ethiopia stayed free, a symbol of African resistance to colonial rule.
In 1932 Abebe Bikila was born. He would run the Rome Olympic marathon barefoot and win, then win again in Tokyo.
In 1935 Italy invaded. Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations, and returned to his throne after the Second World War.
Meles Zenawi, born in 1955, would lead the rebels who took power in 1991, and rule until his death.
Haile Gebrselassie would win two Olympic golds over ten thousand metres and set world records on track and road.
In 1974 a military junta, the Derg, overthrew the emperor, ending the old empire.
Abiy Ahmed, born in 1976, would become prime minister in 2018 and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
In the early eighties famine struck, and pictures of its suffering moved the world to Live Aid.
From 2020 to 2022, war tore through Tigray in the north.
And on the Blue Nile, Ethiopia built its Grand Renaissance Dam, inaugurated at last in 2025.
From Lucy's footsteps to a dam on the Nile, Ethiopia's story runs deeper than almost any other.
